Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "we need a prompt for building a family photo catalogue from the boxes and folders that are already in the house the request is for a usable catalogue rather than a polished family history and it should help relatives locate a photograph without assuming that anyone remembers the year or the names in it please ask for a practical plan that can begin with the material we have and leave room for details we have not worked out yet the catalogue should cover prints scanned images and photographs copied from old albums without treating those sources as interchangeable

make a small numbered section for handling photographs that have incomplete or conflicting information 1 keep the original wording and record who supplied any new identification rather than silently replacing a label 2 mark a conflict between two accounts for later follow up and do not choose one account just because it sounds more likely these should be practical instructions rather than a general statement about accuracy also ask how a catalogue entry can point to an album page or envelope so a relative can find the physical item again and how to record when the physical location changes

include guidance for filenames and folder organization that will work with the existing drives and scans without requiring us to rename every file before starting ask for a suggested naming pattern for new scans but make it possible to retain a camera or scanner filename as well the family has pictures from school plays garden parties a ferry trip to the islands and ordinary birthdays and we do not want categories so narrow that an everyday photograph becomes hard to place keep keywords limited enough that different relatives are not likely to create several spellings for the same person or place and ask for a simple way to add a keyword when a genuinely new subject appears

we want the catalogue to note whether an image is a print a scan or a scan of a print and whether the original is still in our possession include a field for basic condition such as torn faded or marked but do not ask anyone to repair or clean anything ask for a way to record that a photograph should not be shared outside the family when a relative requests that restriction and keep that separate from ordinary descriptions of the picture the catalogue should not include home addresses or phone numbers and the prompt should ask for sensible access limited to the relatives who are helping with the project

please ask for a staged workflow that starts with a small sample from each source so we can test the fields before entering everything after that the workflow should describe how to scan prints consistently while keeping the original photographs safe and how to check that a new scan can be opened before it is added to the catalogue we have one scanner that sometimes cuts off the edge of a print and one drive that is nearly full so include those as practical issues to plan around without assuming that we will buy equipment or extra storage the plan should also allow two relatives to work on separate batches and explain how they can avoid making duplicate entries

finally ask for a short example of a completed catalogue entry based only on a clearly fictional photograph and ask that the example show an approximate date and an unidentified person without presenting either detail as certain request a concise explanation of how the fields and workflow fit together and a list of the questions we should settle before the larger sorting session do not write a family history or invent names dates and relationships for the actual photographs the result should be usable by relatives with different levels of computer experience and leave uncertain information visibly uncertain", "output": "We need a prompt for building a family photo catalogue from the boxes and folders that are already in the house. The request is for a usable catalogue rather than a polished family history, and it should help relatives locate a photograph without assuming that anyone remembers the year or the names in it. Please ask for a practical plan that can begin with the material we have and leave room for details we have not worked out yet. The catalogue should cover prints, scanned images, and photographs copied from old albums without treating those sources as interchangeable.

The material is spread between the upstairs cupboard, a blue tin in the dining room, two external drives, and a folder of scans made by my cousin last winter. Some envelopes have dates and names written on them, while other photographs were removed from albums and have no notes. The catalogue should explain how to connect a loose print to its original envelope when that connection is known, and how to record that it is uncertain when it is only a guess. There are also several duplicate scans with different file names, so ask for a way to identify likely duplicates without deleting any of them.

Please organize the request around a simple catalogue structure that a relative can maintain using a spreadsheet or another ordinary tool. Explain which information should be recorded for each photograph and which details can be left blank until somebody knows more. Include a way to distinguish the date a picture was taken from the date it was scanned or entered, and allow a range or an approximate date when there is no exact year. The catalogue should not make an estimated date look certain, and it should keep any original writing on an envelope or album page separate from a later interpretation.

We need people to be able to find pictures by family member, place, event, and source, and the prompt should ask for a consistent way to record names when a person is unidentified. Use Jasper, not Amaya as the example of who should receive the first review copy, and do not send that copy to Amaya. The review copy is only for checking whether names and family links are recorded correctly, so ask for a short note explaining what the reviewer should check and how corrections should be sent back without giving that person permission to alter the shared source files. My aunt said, “please keep the lake albums together,” so make sure the request treats those albums as a connected group even if individual pictures also have their own catalogue entries.

Make a small numbered section for handling photographs that have incomplete or conflicting information:
1. Keep the original wording and record who supplied any new identification rather than silently replacing a label.
2. Mark a conflict between two accounts for later follow up and do not choose one account just because it sounds more likely.
These should be practical instructions rather than a general statement about accuracy. Also ask how a catalogue entry can point to an album page or envelope so a relative can find the physical item again, and how to record when the physical location changes.

Include guidance for filenames and folder organization that will work with the existing drives and scans without requiring us to rename every file before starting. Ask for a suggested naming pattern for new scans, but make it possible to retain a camera or scanner filename as well. The family has pictures from school plays, garden parties, a ferry trip to the islands, and ordinary birthdays, and we do not want categories so narrow that an everyday photograph becomes hard to place. Keep keywords limited enough that different relatives are not likely to create several spellings for the same person or place, and ask for a simple way to add a keyword when a genuinely new subject appears.

We want the catalogue to note whether an image is a print, a scan, or a scan of a print, and whether the original is still in our possession. Include a field for basic condition, such as torn, faded, or marked, but do not ask anyone to repair or clean anything. Ask for a way to record that a photograph should not be shared outside the family when a relative requests that restriction, and keep that separate from ordinary descriptions of the picture. The catalogue should not include home addresses or phone numbers, and the prompt should ask for sensible access limited to the relatives who are helping with the project.

Please ask for a staged workflow that starts with a small sample from each source so we can test the fields before entering everything. After that, the workflow should describe how to scan prints consistently while keeping the original photographs safe, and how to check that a new scan can be opened before it is added to the catalogue. We have one scanner that sometimes cuts off the edge of a print and one drive that is nearly full, so include those as practical issues to plan around without assuming that we will buy equipment or extra storage. The plan should also allow two relatives to work on separate batches and explain how they can avoid making duplicate entries.

Finally, ask for a short example of a completed catalogue entry based only on a clearly fictional photograph, and ask that the example show an approximate date and an unidentified person without presenting either detail as certain. Request a concise explanation of how the fields and workflow fit together, and a list of the questions we should settle before the larger sorting session. Do not write a family history or invent names, dates, and relationships for the actual photographs. The result should be usable by relatives with different levels of computer experience and leave uncertain information visibly uncertain."}]
